about: Phase 13 evaluation set. Ground truths were written from the evaluation runs (python -m eval.runs: seed 11, 15 min, default traffic; eval_fixed_s11 = fixed timer, eval_rl_s11 = RL agent with the 60 s max-green guard) and from the indexed documents, and only state what those sources say. 'expected' lists the chunks a good retrieval returns: {doc_id, page_label} for documents, {run_id, kind, t} for runs (t = a time inside the window). Scenario items are checked by rules, not by an LLM judge.

questions.question: What happened at 3:41?
questions.ground_truth: At 3:41 a queue spike started on approach N: 12 vehicles were queued while its light was red, 78.9 s after its last green started, during the flashing DON'T WALK of the pedestrian phase that had started at 3:22 with 15 pedestrians waiting. N had 15 arrivals in the previous minute.

questions.question: What was the mean control delay and level of service for the whole run?
questions.ground_truth: The mean control delay was 55.8 s (95th percentile 114.9 s), level of service E; 360 vehicles completed their trips, a throughput of 1440 veh/h.

questions.question: Why did the AI switch at 1:35?
questions.ground_truth: N had been green for 12.9 s and its queue was empty, while E had 7 queued vehicles with the longest wait 59.2 s and S had 8 with 33.9 s. The agent switched to the next phase (E) with P(switch) 99%; a pedestrian call was pending.

questions.question: How confident was the AI when it switched at 13:00?
questions.ground_truth: Not very: P(switch) was 54%. W had been green for 15 s with an empty queue; N had 2 queued with the longest wait 46.3 s and S had 5.

questions.ground_truth: At 0:10 every approach had 0 queued vehicles and 0 s of waiting; N had been green for 10 s and the agent switched with P(switch) 73%, its critic value -1.475. With no one waiting it moved on to the next phase.

questions.question: Is a 120-second cycle too long for a four-leg intersection?
questions.ground_truth: The FHWA Signal Timing Manual says it is preferred that cycle lengths for conventional four-legged intersections not exceed 120 seconds, although larger intersections may require longer cycles, and that cycle lengths that are too long may increase congestion through long waiting queues. So 120 s is at the preferred upper limit.

questions.question: How is the optimum cycle length calculated?
questions.ground_truth: With Webster's model, which minimizes delay when arrivals are random: the optimum cycle length depends on the lost time per cycle (L) and the sum over the phases of the critical lane volume divided by the saturation flow (Y).

questions.question: What walking speed is used to time the pedestrian clearance interval?
questions.ground_truth: The MUTCD uses a walking speed of 3.5 feet per second to the far side of the traveled way or a median; where slower pedestrians or wheelchair users routinely use the crosswalk, a speed below 3.5 feet per second should be considered.

questions.question: How long should the WALK interval be?
questions.ground_truth: The MUTCD says the walk interval should be at least 7 seconds, though as little as 4 seconds may be used when pedestrian volumes are low. The FHWA manual suggests 10 to 15 s in high pedestrian volume areas such as schools or a central business district, 7 to 10 s with typical volumes and longer cycles, and 7 s with typical volumes and shorter cycles.

questions.question: How long should the yellow change interval be?
questions.ground_truth: The MUTCD (Section 4D.26) says a yellow change interval should last at least 3 seconds and at most 6 seconds, with the longer intervals reserved for higher-speed approaches.

questions.question: What is the longest recommended red clearance interval?
questions.ground_truth: The MUTCD says a red clearance interval should not exceed 6 seconds, except when clearing a one-lane, two-way facility or an exceptionally wide intersection.

questions.question: What is passage time in an actuated signal controller?
questions.ground_truth: Passage time (also called passage gap, vehicle extension or unit extension) extends the green for each vehicle actuation, up to the maximum green. When the gap in detector occupancy exceeds the passage time and a call is waiting on a conflicting phase, the phase terminates: a gap out.

questions.question: What minimum green is needed on a major arterial with a speed limit of 40 mph or less?
questions.ground_truth: According to the FHWA manual's driver-expectancy table, 7 to 15 seconds (10 to 15 seconds where the speed limit exceeds 40 mph).

questions.question: What PCU values are used in India for motorcycles and buses?
questions.ground_truth: Kadiyali's Table 8.1 gives 0.50 PCU for a motor cycle, scooter or cycle and 3.00 PCU for a truck or bus (a passenger car or autorickshaw is 1.00).

questions.question: How long is the amber period in Indian signal design?
questions.ground_truth: Kadiyali says the amber period is generally 2 seconds.

questions.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of an exclusive pedestrian phase?
questions.ground_truth: During an exclusive pedestrian phase pedestrians can cross any leg, even diagonally, which reduces conflicts between turning vehicles and pedestrians; the penalty is reduced vehicular capacity and longer cycle lengths, which increase delay for all users. It is not frequently used and is found in central business districts of some cities.

questions.question: How should the maximum green time be set?
questions.ground_truth: One method in the FHWA manual multiplies the minimum-delay green durations of a pre-timed plan by 1.25 to 1.50; at low volumes, when greens rarely reach their maximum, the maximum green can be set fairly high.
